name: Aisha Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate a jumbo, that's a drill rig with two big arms, underground at the Silverline zinc mine. We drill the face for the next blast, about sixty holes in a pattern, then the chargers load them and we clear out. I'm the senior jumbo operator on my shift, so I check the other rigs' patterns and help when someone's stuck. I like getting a clean round where the face breaks exactly to the line, and what wears me out is the noise and the drive down the decline, which is forty minutes each way.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's your life like outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Daniel is an electrician for the local council, and we've got Leo, who's twelve, and Sofia, who's seven. We bought a house five years ago, so the mortgage is the big number. I use an AI app sometimes to help with Leo's homework, mostly so I can check I'm not teaching him maths wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's about what I expected. The stuff is useful for some things and overblown for others. I'd say that at work if it came up, but mostly people would be talking about the football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job is safe for as long as the zinc lasts, which is about fifteen years on the current plan. That's most of my working life. I'd feel fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Keep saving the usual, about three months of bills sitting there now. I might look at the new semi-automatic drilling function the company's been talking about, because it does the pattern for you and saves time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why look at the semi-automatic function if nothing big changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because once a few others have tried it and it works, it's silly not to. I'm not the first to jump, but I don't like being last either. Hassan on the other shift tried it first, and he says it's decent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you spend the time it saves on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, checking the young ones' patterns. A bad hole costs a whole round. If the rig does the boring part, I can be a better shift lead.

S0.say: I'd say it's about what I expected, useful for some things and overblown for others. It'd come up at work only if people weren't talking about the football.
S0.think: My job is safe for as long as the zinc lasts, about fifteen years on the current plan. That's most of my working life, so I'd feel fine.
S0.do: Carries on and keeps her roughly three months of savings topped up. Tries the rig's semi-automatic drilling function after a colleague tested it, and uses the time saved to check junior operators' patterns.
S0.quote: I'm not the first to jump, but I don't like being last either.
S0.fieldNote: Aisha takes on tools once a trusted colleague has tested them. Her horizon is the mine's fifteen-year life, which she sees as enough. She would use saved time to improve her lead role rather than to cut corners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change how we work and we'd better get on with it. I'd tell people not to panic and not to bury their heads either. That's what I'd say at the crib room and to the shift boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the jumbo goes semi-automatic, then fully, within a few years. That means fewer operators, but someone still has to set up, fix and oversee them. I'd want to be that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask the company for training on the automated drill systems and do it as soon as there's a slot. I'd put an extra hundred a fortnight into savings and delay the bathroom renovation. If the mine didn't offer training, I'd start looking at the nearby mines that do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm not scared, but I'm paying attention.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd leave if they didn't train you? That's a big step.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a step I'd take if I had to. There's two other underground mines within an hour, and good jumbo operators are hard to find. I'd rather move once than wait to be pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Daniel think about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say do it, he's always telling me I'm too careful. His job's pretty secure at the council, so that helps. We'd talk it through properly with the numbers before I did anything.

S1.say: I'd say at the crib room and to the shift boss that this will change how we work, so we'd better get on with it. Don't panic, but don't bury your head either.
S1.think: I think the jumbo goes semi-automatic and then fully automatic within a few years, meaning fewer operators. Someone still has to set up, fix and oversee them, and I'd want to be that person.
S1.do: Asks for training on automated drill systems in year one and saves an extra hundred a fortnight, delaying the bathroom renovation. Looks at nearby mines that offer the training if hers doesn't.
S1.feel: Uneasy and alert, but not scared.
S1.quote: I'd rather move once than wait to be pushed.
S1.fieldNote: Aisha's steadiness shows as careful, numbers-first action. She would switch employers to get training, which is a firmer step than her calm tone suggests. Her husband's secure council job gives her room to take that risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan from the government and the companies, quickly, not just speeches. I'd say people need income while they work out what's next. I'd post it, I suppose, which I don't normally do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think there's no 'overseeing the robots' job for long if AI can do everything. I'd be out in a year or two, along with half the mine. Two years doesn't give me time to turn into anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending right away: no renovation, no new car, the holiday cancelled. I'd push our savings from three months towards six. I'd look at Daniel's line of work, electrical, because it might last longer, and see if I could start an apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be up at night checking the bank app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, is an apprenticeship realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, honestly. Apprenticeships take three or four years, and by then who knows. But I'd rather be partway through something than sitting at home waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leo and Sofia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leo would understand, he's twelve and reads everything. I'd tell him money might be tighter for a while but Mum and Dad have it covered. Sofia would just want to know if we're still getting a dog.

S2.say: I'd say we need a real plan from government and companies, quickly, not speeches. People need income while they work out what's next, and I'd even post about it.
S2.think: If AI can do everything, the job of overseeing robots won't last either. I'd be out in a year or two with half the mine, and two years isn't enough to become anything else.
S2.do: Cuts spending at once by cancelling the renovation, new car and holiday, and pushes savings from three toward six months. Looks into an electrical apprenticeship like her husband's, despite doubting it can finish in time.
S2.feel: Alarmed and checking the bank app at night.
S2.quote: I'd rather be partway through something than sitting at home waiting.
S2.fieldNote: Aisha's plan of overseeing the robots disappears under a two-year timeline, and she says so directly. She still chooses to start retraining even though she doubts it will finish in time. The family dog came up as a light moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but workable if we start now. I'd tell people at work to get skills they can take anywhere. I'd want the company to say clearly what the plan is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years gives me time to get a trade, probably electrical. I'd still lose the jumbo, but I'd have something. That's a big difference from the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd sign up for an adult electrical apprenticeship, maybe part time if the mine allows. We'd overpay the mortgage a bit each month. I'd do the automated drill training anyway, because it keeps me useful for a couple more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's the useful kind. I'd feel I was doing something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly does the extra three years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes whether I finish. With two I'd start something and maybe not finish. With five I come out the other side with a ticket, and Daniel can help me with the bits I'm slow on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said electrical might last longer. What if it doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then at least I'll know how to fix my own house. I'm not certain about anything here. I just think robots need wiring and people need power.

S3.say: I'd say five years is short but workable if we start now. I'd tell people at work to get skills they can take anywhere and ask the company for a clear plan.
S3.think: Five years is enough to get a trade, probably electrical, even though I'd still lose the jumbo. That's a big difference from the two-year picture.
S3.do: Signs up for a part-time adult electrical apprenticeship in year one and overpays the mortgage each month. Does the automated drill training too, to stay useful at the mine for a couple more years.
S3.feel: Anxious in a useful way, with a sense of doing something.
S3.quote: With five I come out the other side with a ticket, and Daniel can help me with the bits I'm slow on.
S3.fieldNote: For Aisha the gap between two and five years is whether she finishes a qualification. She is open about not being sure electrical work will last. Her husband is both her model and her tutor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly, and the companies and governments should be planning now. I'd tell people not to wait until the last couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'd be 53, and I could do a full trade and still have a decade of work after. I'd probably take it slower, see what others do first. But I wouldn't sit still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the jumbo for now and start the electrical apprenticeship in a year or two, once I've seen how it's going for others who started first. We'd keep saving steadily and maybe finally do the bathroom. I'd also make sure Leo's thinking about a trade or study that won't vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. It feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd see what others do first. Isn't that a risk with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small one. A year of watching isn't going to sink me with ten years. I just don't like being the guinea pig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Leo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something where he works with people, or fixes things. He loves building stuff. I'd tell him to look at engineering, and if that's too much, a trade.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly, so companies and governments should plan now. I'd tell people not to leave it to the last couple of years.
S4.think: At 53 I could finish a full trade and still have a decade of work after. I'd take it slower and watch others first, but I wouldn't sit still.
S4.do: Keeps the jumbo and starts an electrical apprenticeship in a year or two, after watching others go first. Saves steadily, finally does the bathroom, and steers her son toward engineering or a trade.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, but it feels manageable.
S4.quote: A year of watching isn't going to sink me with ten years. I just don't like being the guinea pig.
S4.fieldNote: Given a decade, Aisha falls back on her habit of watching first, but with a firm plan behind it. She thinks about her son's path as part of the household's response. Her tone stays practical and even.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I like to plan, and that one doesn't give you time to plan anything. What would help is help paying for an apprenticeship as an adult, and some income while you're doing it, because nobody can live on an apprentice wage with a mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask how it feels underground with fewer people. If something goes wrong down there, you want a person next to you, not a sensor. I'd worry about safety for whoever is left.

headlineQuote: If something goes wrong down there, you want a person next to you, not a sensor.
portrait: Aisha Reyes is a 43-year-old senior jumbo operator at the Silverline underground zinc mine, married to a council electrician, with two children and a mortgage. She picks up tools once a colleague has proved them and plans everything with the numbers first. In the steady picture she'd seek training on automated drills, even moving mines to get it, and with five or ten years she would retrain as an electrician. The two-year AGI picture alarms her because it takes away the time she needs to plan and finish anything.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because she likes to plan and it leaves no time to plan anything.
whatWouldHelp: Help paying for an adult apprenticeship and income support while doing it, since nobody can live on an apprentice wage with a mortgage.
